Required Correction: Accurate. NIST classifies SMS/PSTN-delivered OTPs as 'restricted' authenticators specifically because of SIM-swap and number-porting risk — an attacker who takes over the phone number receives the SMS codes instead of the account owner. No correction needed.

Article Title: How Two-Factor Authentication Actually Stops the Most Common Account Hacks
Claim: Authenticator apps generate a new 6-digit code every 30 seconds, entirely on your device, with no network request involved.

Required Correction: Matches the TOTP standard exactly — a 6-digit code derived from a shared secret and the current time via HMAC, refreshed on a 30-second step, computed locally with no network call needed. No correction needed.

Article Title: How Two-Factor Authentication Actually Stops the Most Common Account Hacks

Required Correction: Accurate. FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys are phishing-resistant because authentication is cryptographically bound to the exact requesting domain (origin binding), so a fake look-alike site cannot obtain a valid response. NIST rates this at Authenticator Assurance Level 3 (AAL3), the highest tier, and CISA describes it as the 'gold standard' for MFA. No correction needed.

Advance tax is due in four cumulative instalments: 15% by 15 June, 45% by 15 September, 75% by 15 December, and 100% by 15 March, and applies to anyone with an estimated annual tax liability above ₹10,000. Freelancers/professionals filing under presumptive taxation (Sections 44AD/44ADA) get a concession — they may pay 100% in a single instalment by 15 March. Article should state these actual dates since it warns about 'miscalculating' without ever giving the calendar.

Source: Income Tax Department, Government of India — Section 112A of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as amended by the Finance Act 2024 / Union Budget 2024)
Required Correction: The general point (identical rules apply to both) is correct, but the article omits the actual numbers, which is exactly the gap it was flagged for on a YMYL topic. Current rule: long-term capital gains on equity shares/equity-oriented mutual fund units (STT paid) held over 12 months are taxed at 12.5% on gains exceeding ₹1.25 lakh per financial year, effective for transfers on or after 23 July 2024 (Budget 2024/Finance Act 2024). This replaced the earlier 10% rate above a ₹1 lakh exemption. Short-term capital gains (under 12 months) on the same instruments are taxed at 20%. The editorial note's proposed figure — 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh — is correct and current as of August 2026 and should be stated explicitly in the article.

Article Title: SIP vs Lump Sum: How to Actually Decide Where to Put Your Money

Source: Income Tax Act, 1961 — Section 2(42A) read with Section 112A (holding-period rules for mutual fund units)
Required Correction: Accurate — each SIP instalment is legally treated as an independent purchase for holding-period purposes, so its own 12-month LTCG clock starts from that instalment's specific transaction date. No correction needed.

Article Title: SIP vs Lump Sum: How to Actually Decide Where to Put Your Money
Claim: Historically, markets rise more often than they fall over long periods, so on average, investing immediately has outperformed spreading it out; Lump sum investing has historically outperformed SIP on average, simply because markets rise more often than they fall over time.
Source: Vanguard Research — 'Cost averaging: invest now or temporarily hold your cash?' (US/UK/Australia markets, rolling periods 1976-2022)
Required Correction: Directionally correct globally — Vanguard's research found lump-sum investing beat dollar-cost-averaging in roughly 62-74% of rolling one-year periods across the US, UK, and Australia (1976-2022), because markets rise more often than they fall. However, this is global/developed-market data comparing lump sum vs. DCA of the same cash pool, not an India-specific finding, and it doesn't map cleanly onto India's SIP-from-salary pattern. An India-specific 23-year rolling-return backtest on the Nifty 50 (704 rolling windows) found results much closer to a coin flip depending on horizon: SIP won ~52% of 5-year windows while lump sum won ~52% of 15-year windows, with average return gaps of only 0.5-1.5%. The article's blanket, source-free claim should be qualified — the lump-sum edge is well-established in long-run US/global data but is thinner and horizon-dependent in Indian market data specifically, and no source is currently cited in the article at all.

Banks must credit the disputed amount within 10 working days of notification. The article's framing that a self-authorized/tricked transaction is simply 'treated differently' understates that scam victims who were tricked into authorizing (OTP/UPI PIN entry) can still fall under zero/limited liability if they report within these specific windows — the current vague text risks readers concluding they have no protection once they 'technically authorized' the payment, which is not accurate. Claim: Bitwarden's free tier is usable and has no meaningful feature gate.
Source: Bitwarden — Personal pricing page
Required Correction: None — the free plan covers unlimited passwords on unlimited devices, sync across browser/desktop/mobile/web, passkeys, generator, and breach reports with no artificial cap, matching the article's claim.

Article Title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
Claim: Make the master password a random-feeling but memorable phrase of 4 to 5 unrelated words rather than a short complex string.
Source: NIST SP 800-63B guidance / Diceware passphrase entropy analysis
Required Correction: Passphrases beat short complex strings, which is correct, but 4-5 random words is on the low end specifically for a master password protecting an entire vault; security guidance (Diceware/EFF-style wordlists) commonly recommends 6 words (~78 bits) as the floor for a master password, since 4 words can fall below 64 bits of entropy. Recommend bumping the guidance to 5-6 words minimum for this specific password.

Article Title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
Claim: Reputable password managers use zero-knowledge encryption: the vault is encrypted/decrypted locally with the master password, so even if the company's servers were breached, an attacker would get only encrypted data, and the company itself never has access to the master password.
Source: Bitwarden — Inside zero-knowledge encryption
Required Correction: The core zero-knowledge claim (master password never leaves the device, provider stores only ciphertext) is accurate for reputable managers like Bitwarden and 1Password. However, independent research (e.g., an ETH Zurich analysis) found server-side attack vectors in Bitwarden, LastPass and Dashlane that could, in some scenarios, let a malicious/compromised server undermine guarantees. Soften the absolute framing slightly to note zero-knowledge reduces but does not eliminate all server-side risk.

Article Title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
Claim: A growing number of sites now support passkeys, and most major password managers already store and sync these alongside traditional passwords.
Source: Bitwarden — Personal pricing page (passkeys listed as a free-tier feature)
Required Correction: None — passkey storage/sync is confirmed as a standard feature in Bitwarden's free tier and is broadly available in other major managers (1Password, Google Password Manager, Apple Keychain).

Article Title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
Claim: A small number of sites, particularly some Indian banking and government portals, disable autofill or paste functionality on their login fields for security reasons.
Source: Multiple reports on Indian bank netbanking portals blocking password paste (e.g., IBTimes India, Troy Hunt's "Cobra Effect" writeup)
Required Correction: None — this is a well-documented, longstanding practice among several Indian bank netbanking portals (blocking copy/paste on login fields), though it is increasingly criticized by security researchers as counterproductive.

Article Title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
Claim: Most password managers offer a family or team plan with secure sharing features that let you share a login without revealing the plaintext password to the other person.
Source: Bitwarden — Personal pricing page (Families plan)
Required Correction: None — Families/Teams plans with encrypted item sharing are standard across major password managers (Bitwarden, 1Password, Dashlane).

Article Title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
Claim: The fifteen-minute setup fits inside that window for the overwhelming majority of people, and once done it becomes essentially a one-time cost that runs itself passively.
Required Correction: Time estimate is a subjective/typical-case claim, not independently verifiable; no correction needed, though the article itself concedes this varies with password history size.

Article Title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
Claim: UPI has two request types: a Pay request (you send money) and a Collect request (someone else asks you to authorize sending them money, requiring your PIN to approve); most of the article's scam scenarios (fake refund, QR-code 'receive payment' trick) rely on victims approving a Collect request.
Source: NPCI circular (July 29, 2025) and subsequent reporting on discontinuation of P2P UPI Collect requests
Required Correction: NPCI discontinued person-to-person (P2P) UPI Collect Requests effective October 1, 2025, specifically to curb collect-request fraud; merchant collect requests are unaffected. The article (targeting an August 2026 publish date) needs updating: the general Pay-vs-Collect / 'PIN never needed to receive money' principle still holds, but scenarios framed as an individual (a fake refund sender, an OLX buyer) sending a P2P Collect request are no longer how the scam can be executed on current UPI rails — the scam vector has likely shifted to merchant-disguised or QR-triggered Collect requests, which the article should clarify.

Article Title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
Claim: A common OLX-style scam has a 'buyer' ask a seller to scan a QR code and enter their PIN to 'receive' payment, which actually sends money out via a Collect request.
Source: NPCI circular on P2P Collect Request discontinuation, October 1, 2025
Required Correction: This specific QR-triggered P2P Collect scam mechanism was disrupted by NPCI's October 2025 discontinuation of person-to-person Collect Requests. The underlying warning (scanning a QR/entering a PIN is always a payment, never a receipt) remains valid and should be kept, but the mechanism description needs a note that NPCI has since restricted this exact P2P pathway.

Article Title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
Claim: No bank, UPI app, or NPCI representative will ever ask for your PIN, OTP, CVV, or app password over a phone call, SMS, or chat, for any reason.
Source: RBI/bank consumer-fraud advisories (widely republished, e.g., via RBI cybersecurity awareness communications and bank customer-alert pages)
Required Correction: None — this is standard, consistently repeated official guidance from RBI and Indian banks: PIN/OTP/CVV are never requested by legitimate bank or NPCI staff over call, SMS, or chat.

Article Title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
Claim: Fake customer care numbers walk victims through installing AnyDesk or TeamViewer, giving scammers screen access or control; no genuine bank/UPI support process requires installing a remote-access app.
Source: RBI warning on AnyDesk-based fraud (reported by The Week, Zeebiz, CIO.inc)
Required Correction: None — RBI issued an explicit alert to banks and customers about AnyDesk (and similar apps like TeamViewer, QuickSupport) being used by fraudsters posing as bank staff to gain remote device access; the mechanism described matches reporting closely.

Article Title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
Claim: Report fraud on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) or call 1930 within a few hours, as speed materially affects recovery chances.
Source: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal / 1930 helpline (I4C, Ministry of Home Affairs)
Required Correction: None — 1930 is the correct, current 24/7 national cyber-fraud helpline (it replaced the earlier 155260 number), developed with RBI and banks, and cybercrime.gov.in is the correct portal; speed of reporting genuinely affects the 'golden hour' fund-freezing window.

Article Title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
Claim: A live voice call creates more social pressure and urgency than a text message, which is why voice scams feel more convincing.
Required Correction: General psychological observation, not a specific checkable statistic; no correction needed.

Article Title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
Claim: India's instant-loan-app fraud problem got bad enough that the RBI issued specific digital lending guidance for it.
Source: RBI Guidelines on Digital Lending, 2022 (and subsequent 2025 Digital Lending Directions)
Required Correction: None — RBI issued the Digital Lending Guidelines on August 10, 2022 (effective for new customers from September 2, 2022, existing loans by November 30, 2022), specifically in response to predatory app-based lending; consolidated into RBI's 2025 Digital Lending Directions.

Article Title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
Claim: The RBI maintains a public list of registered NBFCs on its website (rbi.org.in) that can be searched by the exact lending entity's name to verify a loan app.
Source: RBI website / RBI Digital Lending Apps (DLA) directory guidance
Required Correction: RBI does not publish a single list titled 'RBI Approved Loan Apps.' What it maintains is (a) a searchable register of licensed NBFCs/banks, and (b) a separately operationalised Digital Lending Apps (DLA) directory listing apps used by regulated entities. The article's instruction to 'search the RBI's NBFC list' is directionally correct but should be corrected to clarify readers must search for the registered lending entity/NBFC name (as disclosed in the app), not the app's own brand name, since RBI's list is entity-based, not app-name-based.

Article Title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
Claim: RBI's digital lending guidelines require every regulated lender to have a named grievance redressal officer whose contact details are disclosed within the app.
Source: RBI NBFC grievance redressal requirements / RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS) digital lending provisions
Required Correction: None — RBI requires every regulated entity (and its lending service provider) engaged in digital lending to designate a Grievance Redressal Officer/Nodal Officer with published contact details, and this is a mandatory 'Day 0' escalation step before a complaint can go to the RBI Ombudsman.

Article Title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
Claim: Digital lending guidelines require regulated lenders to offer a cooling-off or look-up period, typically a few days, during which a borrower can exit by repaying only principal and proportionate interest, without penalty.
Source: RBI Guidelines on Digital Lending, 2022
Required Correction: None, though could be more precise: RBI mandates a minimum 3-day cooling-off period for loans with tenor of 7 days or more, and a minimum 1-day period for loans with tenor under 7 days, during which the borrower can exit by paying only principal plus proportionate APR.

Article Title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
Claim: Report harassment to the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) or call 1930, and separately file a complaint with the RBI if the lender claims to be a registered NBFC, since RBI has a formal grievance process for regulated entities.
Source: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (1930 helpline) and RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme
Required Correction: None — 1930/cybercrime.gov.in are correct, and RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme is the correct formal channel, but note it requires exhausting the lender's own internal Grievance Redressal Officer first (30-day window) before escalating to the RBI Ombudsman — the article could make this sequencing clearer.

Article Title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
Claim: A fraudulent loan taken through one of these apps can still get reported to credit bureaus in some cases if the lender has even informal bureau reporting arrangements, and unresolved default status can damage your credit score.
Required Correction: Could not find an authoritative source confirming unregistered/fraudulent (non-RBI-regulated) loan apps have working credit bureau reporting arrangements — bureaus like CIBIL/Experian/CRIF/Equifax generally only accept data feeds from RBI-regulated 'Credit Institution' members, which unregistered fraudulent apps by definition are not. The claim risks misleading readers into overestimating a fake app's ability to formally damage their credit file; soften to note this is uncommon/disputed rather than presenting it as a confirmed 'can still happen' risk, or remove unless a specific documented case is cited.

Article Title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
Claim: A regulated lender's onboarding uses Aadhaar-based e-KYC through UIDAI's own system rather than a generic upload field.
Source: UIDAI e-KYC framework used by RBI-regulated lenders
Required Correction: None — Aadhaar-based e-KYC via UIDAI's authentication system is the standard onboarding flow for RBI-regulated digital lenders and NBFCs.

Article Title: Power Bank Buying Guide: What the mAh Number Does Not Tell You
Claim: A power bank typically delivers somewhere around 60 to 75 percent of its rated mAh as actual usable charge through the USB port.
Source: Power bank efficiency analyses (Anker/eufy support documentation; independent power bank testing writeups)
Required Correction: Most sources cite typical realistic usable output closer to 60-70% of rated capacity after 3.7V-to-5V boost conversion and PMIC losses (some low-quality units as low as 65% or worse); the article's upper bound of 75% is achievable with a high-efficiency boost converter (~85-92% efficient) but is on the optimistic edge rather than the typical case. Consider tightening the stated range to roughly 60-70% as the norm, noting 75%+ is possible only with premium components.

Article Title: Power Bank Buying Guide: What the mAh Number Does Not Tell You
Claim: A BIS certification mark has been mandatory for power banks sold in India for several years now, since regulations tightened.
Source: BIS Compulsory Registration Scheme for power banks, IS 13252 (Part 1):2010
Required Correction: None — BIS registration for power banks became mandatory effective May 13, 2015 under the Compulsory Registration Scheme, confirming the article's 'mandatory for several years' framing (over a decade as of 2026); note a transition to the newer IS/IEC 62368-1:2023 standard runs until November 1, 2028.

Article Title: Power Bank Buying Guide: What the mAh Number Does Not Tell You
Claim: DGCA/BCAS rules allow power banks only in cabin baggage, never checked baggage, and cap them at 100 watt-hours (roughly 27000mAh at nominal voltage) without special airline permission.
Source: DGCA Civil Aviation Requirements on carriage of lithium batteries/power banks
Required Correction: None — power banks/spare lithium batteries must be in cabin baggage only; up to 100Wh is allowed without airline approval, 100-160Wh requires prior airline approval, and above 160Wh is prohibited entirely, matching the article's figures. The mAh-to-Wh math (100Wh ÷ 3.7V × 1000 ≈ 27,027mAh) checks out correctly.

Article Title: Power Bank Buying Guide: What the mAh Number Does Not Tell You
Claim: The cells inside a power bank run at roughly 3.7 volts, and you can estimate Wh by multiplying mAh by 3.7 and dividing by 1000.
Source: Standard lithium-ion cell nominal voltage specification (Wh = mAh × V ÷ 1000)
Required Correction: None — 3.7V is the standard nominal voltage for lithium-ion/lithium-polymer cells used in power banks, and the Wh = (mAh × V) ÷ 1000 formula is the correct standard conversion used by airlines and manufacturers.

Article Title: Power Bank Buying Guide: What the mAh Number Does Not Tell You
Claim: A power bank with two or three output ports does not give each port its full rated wattage simultaneously; total output is shared across ports.
Source: General power bank/USB power-delivery specification behavior (shared internal power budget across multi-port designs)
Required Correction: This is standard, widely-understood electrical behavior for multi-port power banks (shared internal power budget) but no single authoritative primary source was found beyond general manufacturer spec-sheet documentation; treat as an industry-standard technical fact rather than one needing a specific citation.

Article Title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
Claim: Browser extensions and price-tracking tools that log a product's price over weeks or months exist, and several of them work on Amazon India and Flipkart listings.
Source: BuyHatke Price History / PriceHistory.app / other India-focused price trackers
Required Correction: None — multiple functioning tools (BuyHatke, Price History, ProductHistory, PriceBefore) specifically track Amazon India and Flipkart price history and offer alerts, confirming the claim.

Article Title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
Claim: Countdown timers that reset after refreshing, or 'only 2 left' labels that persist across days, are a common tactic and should not influence a purchase decision.
Source: India's Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 (CCPA, Consumer Protection Act 2019)
Required Correction: None, but the article misses an opportunity to cite this directly: India's CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns (2023) explicitly name 'false urgency' — including countdown timers that reset on refresh — as one of 13 prohibited dark patterns, and the CCPA has since penalized platforms like Zepto, BookMyShow, IndiGo, and others for this. Naming this regulation would materially strengthen the article's credibility.

Article Title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
Claim: MRP is frequently set high on purpose and rarely reflects what the product sells for even outside sale periods.
Required Correction: General market observation about pricing behavior, not a specific checkable statistic; no correction needed, though a cited example (e.g., a specific product category study) would strengthen it.

Article Title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
Claim: Some sellers briefly list a product at an inflated price for a short window right before a sale starts, purely so the sale price can be measured against that inflated number — a practice sometimes called price anchoring.
Source: Price anchoring / reference-price manipulation practice, discussed in consumer-protection and dark-pattern literature
Required Correction: The mechanism described (a brief price spike right before a sale to inflate the 'before' price) is a recognized manipulative pricing tactic discussed under India's dark-pattern and consumer-protection guidance, though it is more commonly termed 'reference pricing' or 'fake discounting' than 'price anchoring' in Indian regulatory literature specifically. No factual correction needed to the mechanism itself; minor terminology note only.

Article Title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
Claim: A ₹500 'free' bundled accessory that would sell standalone for ₹150 is not really ₹500 of savings, no matter what the bundle page claims.
Required Correction: Illustrative hypothetical example used to make a valid general point about bundle-value inflation; not a specific checkable claim, no correction needed.

Article Title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
Claim: An unusually steep discount from a third-party marketplace seller with few reviews or a recently created storefront carries more risk than the same discount from the platform's own official store.
Required Correction: Reasonable general risk-assessment advice, not a specific statistic; no correction needed.

Article Title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
Claim: A traditional HDD caps sequential speeds around 100 to 160 MB/s, while a SATA SSD pushes sequential speeds around 500 MB/s.
Source: Benchmark discussions of typical 5400/7200 RPM laptop HDD and SATA SSD sequential throughput (Tom's Hardware/PCPartPicker community benchmark data)
Required Correction: None — typical laptop HDDs (5400/7200 RPM) deliver roughly 80-200 MB/s sequential depending on model/RPM, consistent with the article's '100 to 160 MB/s' range, while SATA SSDs commonly reach 500-600 MB/s, matching the article's '~500 MB/s' figure.

Article Title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
Claim: NVMe SSDs are faster than SATA SSDs on paper, sometimes by four to six times in raw sequential speed.
Source: NVMe vs SATA SSD benchmark comparisons (IBM, GigeNET, TechCompare)
Required Correction: A '4-6x' gap is a reasonable description for typical/budget PCIe Gen3 NVMe drives (roughly 2,000-3,500 MB/s vs. ~550-600 MB/s SATA), but high-end Gen4/Gen5 NVMe drives reach 7,000-14,000+ MB/s, a 12-25x gap — larger than the article states. Since this article targets budget laptops, the 4-6x figure is defensible for the relevant drive class, but the phrase 'on paper' slightly understates how large the gap can get on premium NVMe hardware; consider clarifying this is specifically about entry-level NVMe drives.

Article Title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
Claim: eMMC is technically flash storage but noticeably slower than a real SSD, closer to a fast HDD than to SATA SSD speeds.
Source: eMMC vs SSD vs HDD speed comparisons (Windows Central, CDW, Spacehop)
Required Correction: eMMC typically delivers roughly 200-400 MB/s sequential, which is meaningfully faster than most laptop HDDs (80-200 MB/s) but far below SATA SSD (500-600 MB/s). The article's framing ('closer to a fast HDD than to SATA SSD speed') somewhat understates eMMC's real advantage over HDD in raw sequential throughput — the more accurate summary is that eMMC sits clearly between HDD and SATA SSD, but its poor random I/O and lack of a real controller make it feel much closer to HDD in everyday responsiveness, which the article correctly emphasizes elsewhere.

Article Title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
Claim: SSDs slow down as they fill up; keeping at least 10-15% of an SSD free helps it maintain its performance advantage over time.
Source: SSD TRIM/overprovisioning performance guidance (Seagate, Phison, The SSD Review)
Required Correction: None — sources broadly converge on keeping roughly 10-20% of an SSD free (many recommend staying under ~80-85% full) to preserve TRIM/garbage-collection headroom and avoid write-amplification slowdowns; the article's 10-15% figure sits comfortably within this consensus range.

Article Title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
Claim: A laptop with an HDD boots in over a minute versus under 20 seconds for one with an SSD.
Required Correction: Presented as a general illustrative figure without a citation or specific test methodology (OS, hardware generation, background startup apps all affect boot time significantly). Directionally correct that SSDs boot dramatically faster, but the specific numbers ('under 20 seconds' vs 'over a minute') should either be sourced to a specific benchmark/model comparison or softened to avoid implying a precise, universal figure.

Article Title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
Claim: Swapping in a SATA SSD is often a bigger felt improvement than a RAM upgrade on the same machine.
Required Correction: Comparative subjective judgment about perceived performance improvement, not independently checkable as stated; no correction needed, though it aligns with common enthusiast/repair-shop consensus for storage-bottlenecked systems.

Article Title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
Claim: On a tight budget, prioritizing SSD over RAM over CPU generation, in that order, tends to produce the most noticeable everyday improvement per rupee spent.
Required Correction: A prioritization recommendation/value judgment, not a specific checkable fact; no correction needed.

Article Title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
Claim: Checking the IMEI against India's Central Equipment Identity Register (CEIR) tells you whether a device has ever been reported lost, stolen, or blacklisted.
Source: CEIR / Sanchar Saathi (Department of Telecommunications, Government of India)
Required Correction: None — CEIR (now integrated into the Sanchar Saathi portal, ceir.sancharsaathi.gov.in) lets citizens verify IMEI status (valid/blacklisted/duplicate) and also lets owners block/report lost or stolen phones. Article could add the exact portal name (Sanchar Saathi) since 'ceir.gov.in' redirects there and the branding has changed.

Article Title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
Claim: iPhones show battery health, including cycle count, directly under Settings > Battery > Battery Health.
Source: Apple Support
Required Correction: None for older/current iPhones broadly — accurate. Minor nuance: on iPhone 15 and later running iOS 17.4+, cycle count is shown directly in Settings > Battery > Battery Health; on iPhone 14 and earlier, or older iOS versions, cycle count requires the Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics Data workaround since it isn't shown on-screen by default. Article should note this model/iOS-version caveat rather than implying it's uniformly on-screen for all iPhones.

Article Title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
Claim: A brand-new phone's battery should show at or very close to 100 percent health with zero, one, or two charge cycles.
Source: Apple Support (battery and performance documentation)
Required Correction: Directionally correct and consistent with how battery health/cycle count is defined, but no manufacturer publishes an official 'must be 100% with 0-2 cycles to count as new' threshold — a phone that sat in a warehouse or was demoed briefly can legitimately show a handful of cycles and slightly under 100% without being refurbished. Soften to 'should be very close to' rather than implying an exact pass/fail number.

Article Title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
Claim: Flipkart and Amazon India both specify a return or replacement window per listing, and it is frequently shorter for phones, sometimes as little as seven days.
Source: Flipkart Return Policy page; reporting on Amazon India's smartphone return policy change
Required Correction: Flipkart's own policy confirms a 7-day replacement window for mobile phones (15-day return for select premium phones, excluding iPhone/Google Pixel from returns). Amazon India has moved further than the article implies: for most mobile phones Amazon now offers replacement-only (no refund-return) for confirmed manufacturing defects, not a simple 'return window' — the article should clarify replacement vs. return distinction rather than treating both platforms as offering the same kind of window.

Article Title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
Claim: Imported/international-variant refurbished units sold as domestic stock can lack official Indian warranty support entirely and can differ in supported network bands.
Source: General consensus across manufacturer warranty terms (e.g., Apple, Samsung region-locked warranty policies) — no single authoritative Indian government source found
Required Correction: The underlying mechanism (region-locked warranty, band variance) is well established industry practice, but no single official regulator source lists which specific bands or warranty exclusions apply across brands, so this should be treated as generally accurate but not centrally documented — attribute to 'varies by brand and model' rather than a blanket rule.

Article Title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
Claim: A price below the standard street price for that exact model, outside a known sale event, is the single strongest signal something is off.
Required Correction: Editorial judgment/heuristic, not an independently checkable fact. Reasonable advice but presented with more certainty ('the single strongest signal') than can be substantiated.

Article Title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
Claim: Check the factory screen protector for bubbling, the back glass under angled light for micro-scratches, and the charging port for dust or wear as physical tells of prior use.
Required Correction: Practical, plausible advice but subjective/anecdotal rather than a verifiable standard — no authoritative source defines these as reliable refurbishment indicators, and the article itself concedes they're 'not conclusive alone.'

Article Title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
Claim: Genuine new phones ship with a specific, documented set of accessories for that exact model and region, and a missing cable or generic charger is a sign of swapped packaging.
Required Correction: Generally sound consumer advice but not an independently checkable statistic — box contents vary by region/regulatory changes (e.g., many brands no longer ship chargers at all in some markets), so the claim should note that 'no charger in box' is now often normal, not automatically a red flag.

Article Title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
Claim: Electron-based apps (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Notion) can individually use several hundred megabytes to over a gigabyte of memory just sitting open in the background.
Source: Multiple independent reporting/benchmarks (Hacker News discussion threads, technical write-ups on Electron memory usage) — no single vendor publishes official idle-RAM figures
Required Correction: None on the range itself — widely and consistently reported that Slack/Discord/Teams commonly sit at 400MB-2GB+ after some use, consistent with the article's 'several hundred MB to over a gigabyte' framing. Note this is an industry-observation claim, not something with one authoritative source, since Electron/vendors don't publish official memory-use specs.

Article Title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
Claim: Every open browser tab runs largely as its own process with its own memory allocation, and extensions add further overhead.
Source: Google Chrome multi-process architecture documentation
Required Correction: None — Chromium's (and by extension Chrome/Edge/Brave) documented multi-process architecture assigns separate renderer processes per tab/site-instance by default, which is the technical basis for the claim. Firefox uses a similar but more limited multi-process model, so 'largely as its own process' is accurate as a generalization across major browsers.

Article Title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
Claim: Windows Task Manager's Memory tab and macOS Activity Monitor both show real-time usage broken down by app and process, sortable by memory.
Source: Microsoft Support (Task Manager) and Apple Support (Activity Monitor)
Required Correction: None — both are documented, built-in system utilities and both support sorting the process list by memory usage.

Article Title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
Claim: When physical RAM fills up, the OS uses disk space as swap/virtual memory, which is dramatically slower than real RAM even on a fast SSD.
Source: Established computer architecture principle (documented across OS vendor and hardware technical documentation)
Required Correction: None — this is a well-established, non-controversial computing fact: even the fastest consumer NVMe SSDs are orders of magnitude slower than RAM in latency, so swap usage causes noticeable slowdown. No single citable URL needed as this is foundational computer science, not a disputed or vendor-specific claim.

Article Title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
Claim: A large share of modern thin-and-light laptops solder RAM directly to the motherboard, meaning there is no upgrade path after purchase.
Source: General industry knowledge (widely reported across laptop teardown/reviews, e.g., ultrabooks and MacBooks since 2020 using soldered LPDDR RAM) — no single regulator or vendor index tracks 'share' of models
Required Correction: Directionally accurate — soldered RAM is now standard on most premium/thin-and-light lines (MacBooks, XPS, many ultraportables), but 'a large share' is an estimate with no precise industry-wide statistic behind it, and many budget/business laptops (ThinkPad, some HP/Dell lines) still ship with SO-DIMM slots. Soften the claim to avoid implying a specific measured proportion.

Article Title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
Claim: 8GB is workable for basic browsing/office work but tight for multitasking; 16GB is the comfortable baseline for most users in 2026; 32GB is needed for local AI inference, video editing, VMs/Docker, or heavy multitasking.
Required Correction: This is an editorial recommendation/buying-guide judgment, not an independently checkable fact — reasonable given the Electron/browser memory data above, but presented as a settled tier system when actual comfortable RAM varies significantly by specific workload and OS.

Article Title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
Claim: Modern versions of Windows, macOS, and ChromeOS all run more background services, indexing, sync processes, and security features than their equivalents did five years ago.
Required Correction: Plausible general trend but no measured, citable comparison (e.g., idle RAM footprint of Windows 10 vs. Windows 11, or macOS versions five years apart) was found to substantiate this as stated. Should be softened to an editorial observation rather than presented as an established fact.

Article Title: Smartwatch Buying Guide: Which Features Are Worth Paying Extra For
Claim: A watch with its own built-in GPS chip can track an outdoor run or ride accurately without the phone nearby; a watch without one relies on the phone's GPS over Bluetooth.
Source: General smartwatch/wearable GPS architecture, consistent across major vendor documentation (Garmin, Apple, Samsung)
Required Correction: None — this is standard, well-documented smartwatch design: 'connected GPS' watches use the paired phone's GPS radio while 'built-in GPS' watches have their own chip and antenna. Consistently described this way across vendor spec sheets.

Article Title: Smartwatch Buying Guide: Which Features Are Worth Paying Extra For
Claim: SpO2 and ECG sensors on consumer smartwatches are useful for spotting trends but aren't certified medical diagnostic devices and shouldn't be treated as one.
Source: Apple (Blood Oxygen app disclaimer) and Samsung (Galaxy Watch health disclaimers)
Required Correction: Accurate for SpO2 (Apple explicitly states Blood Oxygen readings are 'not intended for medical use' and are wellness-only). ECG is a partial exception: Apple Watch's ECG app IS FDA-cleared (De Novo classification) specifically for detecting atrial fibrillation and is a legitimate over-the-counter medical feature for that one purpose — but it explicitly cannot detect heart attacks and isn't a general diagnostic tool. Article should distinguish that ECG has narrow FDA clearance for AFib detection, while SpO2 generally does not have equivalent medical clearance.

Article Title: Smartwatch Buying Guide: Which Features Are Worth Paying Extra For
Claim: An IP68 rating covers dust and splash resistance but isn't built for swimming; a 5ATM rating is tested for sustained water pressure at depth and is what's needed for swimming.
Source: ISO 22810:2010 (water-resistant watches standard); Samsung Global Newsroom
Required Correction: None on the core distinction — IP68 is an ingress-protection (dust/static submersion) test under IEC 60529, while 5ATM/ISO 22810 includes condensation, temperature, and static overpressure testing more relevant to swimming. Worth adding the nuance that even 5ATM is a static-pressure test and doesn't fully account for dynamic forces like diving entry or strong swimming strokes, so brands still often advise against high-impact water sports even at 5ATM.

Article Title: JavaScript Basics: The Concepts Every Beginner Actually Needs

Article Title: How to Turn Off Ads in Free Android Apps — What Is Legal and What Is Not
Claim: Downloading a 'mod APK' that claims to have ads pre-removed is copyright infringement on the developer's side, and violates the terms of service you agreed to when you first installed the real app.
Source: law.asia — Reverse Engineering and India's Copyright Act; SpicyIP — Is Decompilation of Software Legal Under the Indian Copyright Act
Required Correction: Directionally correct — unauthorized reverse-engineering and redistribution of a copyrighted app likely infringes under India's Copyright Act, 1957 (as amended in 2012 to add anti-circumvention/technological-protection-measure provisions), and separately breaches the app's ToS as a contract matter. But the article asserts this as flat legal fact with zero citation to any actual statute or case. It should name the legal basis (Copyright Act 1957, the 2012 anti-circumvention amendment) and note that Indian law does recognize a fair-use/interoperability exception for reverse engineering — which does not cover redistributing a modified app to others, a distinction the article never draws.

Article Title: How to Turn Off Ads in Free Android Apps — What Is Legal and What Is Not
Claim: Using root access to patch out an app's ad SDK for personal use is a gray area, but distributing that patch or the patched app to others crosses clearly into copyright and platform policy violation.
Source: law.asia — Reverse Engineering and India's Copyright Act
Required Correction: Broadly consistent with how Indian copyright law treats unauthorized reproduction/distribution vs. narrower personal-use reverse engineering, but again stated with no citation to the actual statute. Reference the Copyright Act 1957 (as amended) directly instead of asserting the legal conclusion as if self-evident.

Article Title: How to Turn Off Ads in Free Android Apps — What Is Legal and What Is Not
Claim: Network-level ad blocking (apps/Private DNS blocking ad domains) doesn't alter the app's code or violate copyright, and is generally treated as acceptable personal use in India.
Required Correction: No Indian statute, regulation, or case law specifically addressing the legality of DNS/network-level ad blocking could be located. The underlying logic (no code is modified, nothing copyrighted is redistributed) is reasonable, but 'generally treated as acceptable... legal' is stated as settled law with zero citation — the same unsupported-legal-claim pattern flagged for the whole article. Either find a real source discussing ad-blocker legality in India specifically, or reframe this section as informed inference rather than a legal conclusion.

No correction needed; citing the specific policy name would strengthen the article.

Article Title: How to Turn Off Ads in Free Android Apps — What Is Legal and What Is Not

Article Title: How to Actually Stick to a Morning Routine, Based on What Derails Most People

Article Title: Prepaid vs Postpaid Mobile Plans: Which Actually Costs Less Over a Year
